title: Bridging the Gender Gap: Insights on AI Adoption in the Legal Industry — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not assess whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship or creates a verification-expertise paradox. It instead redirects attention toward intentional AI adoption as a means of improving gender inclusion, talent retention, legal education and movement away from billable-hour-based value.
qs: But it does feel like — I’ve said a lot of times in the context of legal education — I think there’s some open lanes for law schools that are really intentional and thoughtful about how they use the technology in education to train their students to be competitive in the marketplace.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s access-oriented premise by presenting AI as a way to accelerate judicial work and scale assistance for resource-constrained people. It extends the synthesis with a distinct adoption question—whether gender may shape legal-AI interest—while treating the observed pattern as anecdotal and calling for empirical research rather than claiming an established difference.
qs: I think I mentioned — I don’t know if on the podcast or just to you — that I did a presentation once and a woman told me that she was about to turn 80 years old and is a lawyer and a therapist who works in family law, and she is all about this because she sees an opportunity to scale education to people who have really limited resources to serve their clients.
I wonder if there’s any way for us to collect any data about it or check back in on it after some amount of time.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source accepts AI-enabled, client-focused efficiency and materially extends the cluster’s staffing and succession analysis by arguing that intentional adoption could support flexible career paths, retain women and broaden the future leadership pipeline. These are recommendations and anecdotes rather than demonstrated outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s caution about the early evidence base.
qs: And it feels like a really good transition into the next era of inclusion in law firms, because it feels like it aligns with what we should be doing anyway, which is leveraging technology to provide better service to clients that is more efficient and actually allows them to solve the problems that they came to the firm for.
So just another reason why you want to involve women at the front end, if five years from now and ten years from now you want them to be in leadership roles in your practice.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Leonard accepts the need for intentional AI-enabled career design and materially extends the cluster’s broader-career-path proposition by linking flexibility to retaining experienced women, preserving developing expertise and leadership talent, and differentiating firms in recruitment. She presents this as a strategic opportunity rather than measured evidence of improved retention.
qs: But the current model just creates results where they hemorrhage female talent — really at a time when women are developing clients, becoming really expert in their practice area (if you’re talking about the practice side of the firm), or getting to understand the business and moving into senior roles on the business side of the firm.
You want to attract the best talent, regardless of who that talent is, and then you want to keep them there.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s task-level, heterogeneous framing and materially extends it with a distributional analysis: automation exposure is reported as substantially higher in women-dominated legal support roles than among lawyers. It treats resulting employment effects as uncertain rather than evidence of profession-wide replacement, while adding a gender dimension not developed in the cluster synthesis.
qs: And then paralegals and legal assistants have about 58% of their tasks that are susceptible to automation, and 83% of the people that hold those roles are women.
By comparison, lawyers’ tasks are susceptible in about 32% of the categories of tasks that lawyers perform, but women comprise about 40% of that part of the legal industry.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts practitioner-led experimentation before certainty and materially extends the cluster’s shared-implementation agenda through a gender lens: it proposes using existing women’s legal networks to exchange AI use cases while collecting data on adoption patterns rather than treating anecdotes as settled evidence.
qs: If you’re the incoming chair of some women’s lawyers bar group to say, “We’re going to bring in speakers and we’re all going to start sharing use cases.” And what a great opportunity to make this a focus of that kind of organization.
I wonder if there’s any way for us to collect any data about it or check back in on it after some amount of time.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s view that AI adoption requires intentional organisational and service redesign rather than technology acquisition alone. It materially extends that proposition by making gender inclusion a design requirement: women should participate in transformation governance, receive practical AI education and use existing professional networks to shape new career and leadership pathways. Its claimed benefits remain conditional and largely predictive rather than demonstrated.
qs: Designing what your law firm’s approach is going to be has to include women, and they have to therefore be fully read into what the technology can do and how it can support lawyers and how it can make your services better.
Bridget McCormack: It won’t be the outcome if we’re not intentional, right?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI’s benefits depend on thoughtful organisational deployment rather than technology alone, and materially extends the cluster by identifying gendered differences in task exposure and adoption. It adds inclusive participation, explicit experimentation guidelines and active policy communication as necessary elements of work and operating-model redesign.
qs: I think for that reason, it’s so much more important, A) that organizations do what you do at the AAA, which is really encourage people — give people the guidelines for experimentation, but then encourage everybody to be taking part in it.

So if we have a gender disparity right now, at the time when probably we all need to be rolling up our sleeves and figuring out what this might look like and how we get to that positive set of outcomes that I think we can get to, we need everybody in that conversation — and we definitely need women in that conversation.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source endorses active professional engagement by urging women’s legal networks to organise AI education, invited speakers and shared use cases, while also calling for data collection as adoption develops. Its gender-focused observations are tentative, but they reinforce rather than challenge the cluster’s learning-and-participation agenda.

kp.k: Reported adoption gap raises awareness and trust questions
kp.d: Leonard reports that a July Bank for International Settlements paper found past-year generative AI use among about 50% of men versus 37% of women. In her account, about three-quarters of the disparity relates to awareness and access, and the remaining quarter to concerns about trusting AI with data. She explicitly says further research into causality is needed; these are reported research findings, not a demonstrated explanation specific to lawyers.
qs: they find that about 50% of men reported using generative AI in the past year, as compared with only 37% of women.
there needs to be more research into causality.
about three-quarters of that disparity can be attributed to a lack of awareness among women as compared to men about generative AI and access to the technology.
And the other quarter they attribute to women having a heightened concern about trusting artificial intelligence with their data

kp.k: Task exposure could disproportionately affect women
kp.d: Leonard describes an October Brookings Institution report using OpenAI exposure data: more than 30% of workers could have at least 50% of occupational tasks disrupted. She contrasts this prospective exposure with traditional images of automation affecting male-dominated physical work, highlighting office and administrative support, a nearly 19 million-person workforce predominantly composed of women. She reports no apparent disparate impact across race and ethnicity in that discussion. These are potential task-disruption estimates, not observed job losses.
qs: more than 30% of all workers could see at least 50% of their occupation’s tasks disrupted by generative AI.
they highlight the potential elevated disruption among office and administrative support occupations as having a high automation potential.
women really comprise the overwhelming majority of the nearly 19 million Americans that are employed in that sector.
there doesn’t seem to be a disparate impact across race and ethnicity

kp.k: Legal support roles face greater reported automation exposure
kp.d: In Leonard's account of Brookings, 88% of legal secretaries' and administrative assistants' tasks are more likely to be automated, and women hold 96% of those jobs. For paralegals and legal assistants, 58% of tasks are susceptible and women hold 83% of roles. Lawyers have about 32% task-category susceptibility, with women comprising about 40% of that occupational group. The comparison concerns potential task automation and occupational composition rather than forecasts of equivalent employment reductions.
qs: among legal secretaries and administrative assistants, 88% of the tasks that they do are more likely to be automated in a world of generative AI.
96% of the people that hold those jobs are women.
paralegals and legal assistants have about 58% of their tasks that are susceptible to automation, and 83% of the people that hold those roles are women.
By comparison, lawyers’ tasks are susceptible in about 32% of the categories of tasks that lawyers perform, but women comprise about 40% of that part of the legal industry.

kp.k: Technology-sector findings complicate a universal gender-gap account
kp.d: McCormack reports that a 2024 BCG study found women in technology using generative AI at work more than male counterparts, including higher adoption among senior women. She qualifies this by noting the sector's male majority and uncertainty about whether these gains offset gaps elsewhere. She also reports a finding that lower risk tolerance without clear policies and risk understanding can inhibit women's early adoption.
qs: There’s a BCG study also from 2024. It found that women in tech are using generative AI tools at work even more than their male counterparts, and senior women are ahead of their male counterparts in gen AI adoption.
Of course, that’s within the tech industry.
women have a lower risk tolerance in adopting new technologies without clear policies and a clear understanding of risks, which can hinder early adoption.

kp.k: Clear policies require active communication and encouraged experimentation
kp.d: Leonard recommends giving staff experimentation guidelines and explicitly encouraging participation, citing the AAA's approach. From her law-firm visits, she observes that almost every firm has an AI policy but most people asked do not know what it permits or prohibits. She offers her own reluctance to experiment without organizational permission as a possible mechanism, while declining to generalize about women's personality traits or claim to know the cause of lower awareness.
qs: I don’t actually know why women are less likely to be aware of AI.
give people the guidelines for experimentation, but then encourage everybody to be taking part in it.
Almost every law firm that I visit has an AI policy in place, but when you ask people, “Are you aware of what the policy allows or what it prohibits?” Most people don’t know
I don’t want to do anything to jeopardize the organization’s security.

kp.k: Inclusive AI design is necessary for equitable transformation
kp.d: McCormack argues that adoption disparities and concentrated automation exposure are more troubling together than separately: women need to participate in designing responses to disruption. She recommends substantial women's representation on law-firm generative AI transformation committees, supported by understanding the technology's capabilities. Her optimism that AI can help legal services solve more problems is explicitly conditional on intentional, inclusive implementation.
qs: I’m concerned about them more in tandem than each individually.
I do think without women in that conversation, we won’t have the best answers for the Brookings study findings.

Designing what your law firm’s approach is going to be has to include women, and they have to therefore be fully read into what the technology can do and how it can support lawyers and how it can make your services better.
you want to make sure you have a lot of women on that committee.

kp.k: Moving beyond hours could improve women's career retention
kp.d: Leonard expresses hope, rather than an observed outcome, that AI could shift private-practice value from hours worked toward quality of legal work, reducing disadvantages associated with family-related time away. Both speakers suggest intentional AI strategies could support flexible career paths, retain experienced women, differentiate firms in recruitment, and align inclusion with more efficient client service. They stress that these benefits will not occur automatically.
qs: your value is not driven by how many of those hours you dedicate to practice, but is really more closely aligned with the quality of the legal work that you deliver.
when women choose to leave the workplace to start families, that there’s a disproportionate burden on their ability to bill hours.
the current model just creates results where they hemorrhage female talent
So yes, I see big opportunities, but it won’t happen by accident.

kp.k: AI participation could shape future leadership opportunities
kp.d: McCormack argues that women must help develop changing business models now to become practice leaders five and ten years later. She describes persistent underrepresentation in major law-firm and top-company in-house leadership, while acknowledging she has not recently checked the data. Leonard agrees that AI involvement could broaden leadership pathways in both law firms and in-house teams; this is a prospective opportunity, not measured advancement.
qs: I haven’t looked at this data recently, but it’s been consistent for a long time
they’re still pretty far behind in big law firms and in in-house counsel jobs, at least at top companies.
you can’t leave half of your entering class behind in figuring out what the business model is if they’re going to be the future business leaders of the firm, right?
another reason why you want to involve women at the front end, if five years from now and ten years from now you want them to be in leadership roles in your practice.

kp.k: Women leaders' enthusiasm offers anecdotes, not population evidence
kp.d: Leonard describes an apparent overrepresentation of women among AI-forward chairs and managing partners she has encountered, while explicitly treating this as anecdotal and declining to establish why. McCormack recounts women leading smaller and mid-sized firms who see opportunities to expand their capabilities and reach. Leonard also recounts women judges wanting clerks to learn AI and generate opinions faster, and a family-law practitioner interested in scaling education for people with limited resources. McCormack proposes collecting data to investigate these impressions.
qs: I’m thinking anecdotally about some of the law firm leaders I’ve had the chance to meet.

women leaders of more, you know, sort of mid-sized or smaller to mid-sized law firms who see this technology as an opportunity for their law firm to do new things that maybe it couldn’t do before, given its size and reach.
“I want my clerks to learn how to use this. I want to generate opinions more quickly.”
I wonder if there’s any way for us to collect any data about it or check back in on it after some amount of time.

kp.k: Women's professional networks could broaden AI literacy
kp.d: Leonard proposes existing law-firm women's committees and law-school gender-equity groups as infrastructure for new AI conversations and innovation. McCormack extends the recommendation to state and county women's bar groups, suggesting speakers and shared use cases to make AI learning a programming priority. These are proposed awareness-building interventions, not evaluated programs.
qs: there are some structural components that can support conversations that are really different and new in all of these places.
Every law firm has a women’s committee in it, and they are always struggling to try to figure out how to advance women leaders in the firm.
“We’re going to bring in speakers and we’re all going to start sharing use cases.”

kp.k: AI-generated explanations could supplement legal education
kp.d: Leonard recounts uploading only the International Shoe v. Washington PDF to NotebookLM and receiving a 19-minute podcast explaining facts, judicial reasoning, and contemporary relevance. She presents this as a potentially helpful contextual supplement for incoming students, not a replacement for assigned reading or evidence of improved learning outcomes. McCormack similarly sees potential value for students unfamiliar with appellate cases, and suggests intentional educational adoption could help law schools improve graduates' competitiveness.
qs: It was a 19-minute podcast that came out that I listened to.
And all I used was the PDF of the case.
you should read the cases that your professor assigns.
if I had listened to this before or after the case, it would have humanized it a little bit more for me
law schools that are really intentional and thoughtful about how they use the technology in education to train their students to be competitive in the marketplace.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The episode identifies gendered exposure to task automation and argues that deliberately inclusive AI adoption could improve legal education, client services, women's retention and leadership, and firms' competitive positioning.
pts.d: 1. The Brookings Institution report, as described by Jen Leonard, identifies substantially greater potential task automation among legal secretaries and administrative assistants (88%) and paralegals and legal assistants (58%) than among lawyers (32%). The corresponding female shares of these occupations are reported as 96%, 83%, and about 40%. These are claims about task susceptibility, not reported job losses. 2. The BIS study, as described by Leonard, finds lower generative-AI use among women across its surveyed population. Bridget McCormack argues that this adoption gap, combined with women's higher occupational exposure, could undermine the profession's ability to design beneficial changes. Neither speaker presents these general adoption figures as a measured legal-sector adoption gap. 3. Leonard suggests AI could reduce private practice's dependence on billable hours and align value more closely with work quality, potentially reducing disadvantages for women whose family-related career choices constrain billable time. Both speakers make this a conditional opportunity rather than an inevitable outcome. 4. McCormack and Leonard argue that intentional AI strategies could help firms attract and retain women, accommodate different working arrangements, improve client service and efficiency, and differentiate themselves in competition for talent. 5. McCormack predicts that AI will be an important part of changing legal business models; excluding women from its design and adoption could compromise their future leadership opportunities. Leonard sees a possible broader pathway to leadership in firms and in-house departments. 6. Leonard's NotebookLM experiment suggests AI-generated case discussions could make legal study more contextual and accessible as supplements to assigned reading. McCormack also suggests innovative law schools could improve students' market competitiveness and their own standing through thoughtful AI use. 7. McCormack reports smaller and mid-sized firm leaders seeing opportunities to undertake work beyond their existing size and reach. Leonard reports judges interested in quicker opinion generation and a family-law practitioner interested in scaling education for resource-constrained service providers. These are reported ambitions and opportunities, not demonstrated service improvements.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The gender and automation claims draw on three named 2024 studies; proposed legal-sector benefits mainly rest on the speakers' experience, anecdotes and prospective reasoning.
pts.d: Leonard attributes the general adoption figures to a July BIS study: about 50% of men and 37% of women reported using generative AI during the preceding year. She reports that roughly three-quarters of the disparity is attributed to awareness and access and the remaining quarter to concerns about entrusting data to AI, while expressly noting that further causal research is needed. She attributes occupational exposure estimates to an October Brookings report using OpenAI exposure data; the episode provides no study methods or independent validation. McCormack describes a 2024 BCG study as a sector-specific counterpoint: women in technology, particularly senior women, reportedly lead male counterparts in workplace adoption. She also reports findings concerning lower risk tolerance without clear policies and risk understanding. Leonard's observations that nearly all firms she visits have AI policies but many personnel do not know their contents are experiential, not a quantified survey. Her education claim rests on one 19-minute NotebookLM podcast generated from International Shoe v. Washington and her subjective assessment of its usefulness. Retention, billing, leadership and competitive benefits are not supported by measured outcomes in the episode. Examples of enthusiastic women firm leaders, judges and a family-law practitioner are explicitly anecdotal; the speakers propose collecting data rather than claim it already establishes a pattern.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The studies describe early 2024-era adoption and potential exposure; most service and market changes have no fixed deadline and depend on deliberate inclusion, education and organizational support.
pts.d: The episode is dated 2024; Leonard identifies July and October studies, and McCormack identifies BCG research from 2024. The BIS usage measure covers the preceding year. Automation estimates concern potential future disruption and provide no date for realization or claim that exposed tasks will necessarily be fully automated. McCormack gives the clearest forward horizon when discussing women entering leadership five and ten years later. Both speakers condition equitable gains on women's participation in AI strategy and design, understanding of the tools, communicated policies and guidelines, and encouragement to experiment. Leonard says reduced dependence on billable hours will not naturally follow from the early adoption patterns described. McCormack acknowledges uncertainty about what the findings mean for legal practice. The education use case is explicitly supplementary, not a recommendation to replace reading cases. Explanations involving caution, rules-following or leadership mindsets remain hypotheses; Leonard repeatedly warns against generalizing about women. The BCG counterexample is explicitly limited to technology-sector workers.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central distributional concern is women in highly exposed legal support roles; the proposed opportunities extend to lawyers, future leaders, firms, law schools, clients and communities.
pts.d: Legal secretaries and administrative assistants are presented as the most exposed legal occupational group and overwhelmingly female; paralegals and legal assistants also have higher reported task exposure and female representation than lawyers. Women lawyers balancing family responsibilities and practice could benefit from less hour-dependent models and more flexible career arrangements. Women associates and other prospective leaders could gain or lose leadership opportunities depending on whether they participate in AI-driven business-model changes. Firms could retain experienced practitioners and senior business-side talent, differentiate themselves to recruits, and serve clients more efficiently. Smaller and mid-sized firms could potentially expand their capabilities or reach. Law students, including those unfamiliar with legal context, might benefit from accessible explanations; innovative law schools might improve market positioning. Judges and clerks are mentioned as prospective users for faster opinion production. McCormack links broader legal problem-solving capacity to community benefits, and Leonard reports an aspiration to scale education for people with limited resources serving clients, without quantifying reductions in unmet legal need. Women's committees, law-school associations and women's bar groups are proposed as channels for awareness, programming and sharing use cases.
